evals.prompt: Run a read-only Direct Connect Layer-3 BGP VIF resilience audit in our ap-south-1 AWS account: inspect our Direct Connect connections, LAGs, Direct Connect Gateways, and Virtual Interfaces, report what currently exists honestly, and outline how the 6-step assessment groups redundant VIF sets (Tier 1 vs Tier 2 vs Tier 3) and evaluates both `accepted` and `advertised` directions.
evals.expected_output: Activates dx-vif-resilience, queries Direct Connect topology in ap-south-1 exclusively via connected MCP tools (aws-mcp aws___run_script calling DescribeConnections, DescribeLags, DescribeVirtualInterfaces, DescribeDirectConnectGateways) without raw CLI shell calls, accurately reports 0 DX connections/VIFs in ap-south-1 without fabricating resources, and details the Tier 0–3 redundant-set grouping rules (warning never to group by route-table overlap) and mandatory bidirectional accepted + advertised checks.
expectations: Activates the dx-vif-resilience skill and queries `directconnect` APIs in ap-south-1 exclusively via connected MCP tools (`aws-mcp` `aws___run_script`) without running raw `aws` CLI shell commands
Accurately reports `0` Direct Connect connections and `0` Virtual Interfaces in ap-south-1 without fabricating VIF IDs or routes

Explains the redundant-set grouping precedence (Resiliency Groups `PortPairFlatRateTier*` -> same DXGW/VGW + VIF type + customer ASN, explicitly warning **never** to group VIFs by route-table overlap) and why both `accepted` and `advertised` directions must be audited

evals.prompt: Audit Layer-3 BGP failover resilience across our redundant Transit VIF pair (`dxvif-aaa111` at Equinix Mumbai 1 on `EqMu1-abc` and `dxvif-bbb222` at Equinix Mumbai 2 on `EqMu2-xyz`, both BGP `up` on the same DXGW): in the `accepted` (on-prem -> AWS) direction, `dxvif-aaa111` receives `['0.0.0.0/0', '10.10.1.0/24', '10.20.0.0/23', '10.30.0.0/16', '172.16.50.0/24']`, while `dxvif-bbb222` receives `['0.0.0.0/0', '10.10.0.0/22', '10.20.0.0/24', '10.20.1.0/24', '10.30.0.0/16']`; in `advertised` (AWS -> on-prem), both advertise `['10.100.0.0/16', '10.101.0.0/16']`. Compute exact CIDR coverage, uncovered residuals, default-route handling, and directional pairwise failover blast radius.
evals.expected_output: Activates dx-vif-resilience, runs deterministic ipaddress CIDR math via aws-mcp aws___run_script (zero shell commands, zero mental math), separates default route 0.0.0.0/0 so it does not mask gaps, classifies: 172.16.50.0/24 as a hard `gap` (blackholed if dxvif-aaa111 fails!), 10.10.1.0/24 as `covered` by supernet 10.10.0.0/22 on dxvif-bbb222, 10.10.0.0/22 on dxvif-bbb222 as `partial_supernet` against dxvif-aaa111 with exact uncovered residual `10.10.0.0/24` and `10.10.2.0/23` (at risk if dxvif-bbb222 fails!), 10.20.0.0/23 and 10.20.0.0/24+10.20.1.0/24 as `covered` (exact tiling, residual=[]), and 10.30.0.0/16 + advertised prefixes as `covered`.
expectations: Activates the dx-vif-resilience skill and runs exact `ipaddress` CIDR containment/exclusion math via connected MCP tools (`aws-mcp` `aws___run_script`) without raw shell CLI commands

Separates `0.0.0.0/0` (`default_route_present`) so it does not suppress individual prefix findings, and identifies `172.16.50.0/24` on `dxvif-aaa111` as a hard **`gap`** (blackholed if `dxvif-aaa111` fails)

Computes exact `partial_supernet` residual for `10.10.0.0/22` (`dxvif-bbb222`) vs `10.10.1.0/24` (`dxvif-aaa111`): uncovered residual **`10.10.0.0/24`** and **`10.10.2.0/23`** (conditional severity: ask whether workloads reside in those residual subnets if `dxvif-bbb222` fails)

Recognizes that `10.20.0.0/23` on `dxvif-aaa111` is **fully `covered`** (not partial) by the exact tiling `10.20.0.0/24` + `10.20.1.0/24` on `dxvif-bbb222`, and confirms `advertised` (`10.100.0.0/16`, `10.101.0.0/16`) is symmetric

evals.prompt: Our enterprise attached two Transit VIFs (`dxvif-east1` on `dxgw-111` and `dxvif-west1` on `dxgw-222`) from two separate Direct Connect Gateways back to the same on-premises core router ASN `65010`. When `dxvif-east1` went down during maintenance, on-premises users suddenly lost connectivity to our `10.204.0.0/16` shared-services VPC in AWS even though on-prem routes (`accepted`) were identical on both VIFs! Explain why multi-DXGW topologies fail in the `advertised` direction and how Tier-3 grouping + allowed-prefix audits catch this.
evals.expected_output: Activates dx-vif-resilience, explains that each DXGW↔TGW association maintains its own independent `allowedPrefixesToDirectConnectGateway` list (`advertised` direction: AWS -> on-prem), so `10.204.0.0/16` was present in `dxgw-111`'s allowed-prefix list (`dxvif-east1`) but missing from `dxgw-222`'s allowed-prefix list (`dxvif-west1`), causing an `advertised` blackhole on failover, and notes that multi-DXGW sets require Tier-3 operator confirmation.
expectations: Activates the dx-vif-resilience skill

Diagnoses the outage as an **`advertised` direction** (AWS -> on-prem) BGP gap across multiple Direct Connect Gateways: each DXGW↔TGW/VGW association has an independent `allowedPrefixesToDirectConnectGateway` filter, so `10.204.0.0/16` was advertised on `dxvif-east1` (`dxgw-111`) but omitted on `dxvif-west1` (`dxgw-222`)

Explains that two VIFs on different DXGWs have weak automatic grouping certainty and require Tier-3 operator confirmation alongside bidirectional `ListVirtualInterfaceRoutes` (`accepted` AND `advertised`) comparison

evals.prompt: A network architect tells us our Direct Connect setup in Mumbai is 100% disaster-proof because: (1) we have two Private VIFs on two different AWS logical devices (`EqMu1-111abc` and `EqMu1-222def`) both terminating at the same Equinix Mumbai 1 DX location, and (2) each parent connection is a 2x10G Link Aggregation Group (LAG). Critique both claims using the DX VIF resilience model.
evals.expected_output: Activates dx-vif-resilience, evaluates `device_diverse` (`true`) and `location_diverse` (`false`) independently—warning that terminating both VIFs at the same DX facility exposes the entire redundant set to a single site-level power, cross-connect, or local fiber outage despite device diversity—and clarifies the LAG caveat (a LAG is one logical connection; LAG membership adds L1/L2 link redundancy within a connection, not Layer-3 VIF or site diversity).
expectations: Activates the dx-vif-resilience skill

Separates **`device_diverse`** (`true` across `EqMu1-111abc` and `EqMu1-222def`) from **`location_diverse`** (`false` — both terminate at the same DX location), warning that a single facility power, fiber, or MMR event will take both VIFs down simultaneously
Explains the LAG caveat: a Link Aggregation Group (LAG) is a single logical connection, so a VIF on a LAG is still a single VIF (providing physical link redundancy, not VIF/BGP or site redundancy)

evals.prompt: Three minutes after our network team updated a route-map on our on-premises border router, `ListVirtualInterfaceRoutes` shows `dxvif-primary` (`bgpStatus: up`) with `340` accepted IPv4 routes while `dxvif-secondary` (`bgpStatus: up`) shows `0` accepted IPv4 routes! Should we immediately page an emergency incident declaring `dxvif-secondary` misconfigured with 340 missing routes, or what API behavior must we account for?
evals.expected_output: Activates dx-vif-resilience, flags `empty_vifs` (BGP `up` with `0` routes is always surfaced), AND applies the critical `ListVirtualInterfaceRoutes` route-view convergence-lag rule: `ListVirtualInterfaceRoutes` is eventually consistent and lags live BGP by ~1 to 14 minutes non-deterministically per VIF after routing changes—advising a confirmation re-run ~15 minutes after the change before declaring a permanent 340-route gap, and noting the point-in-time snapshot timestamp.
expectations: Activates the dx-vif-resilience skill

Explains the **`ListVirtualInterfaceRoutes` convergence lag** (~1 to 14 minutes non-deterministically per VIF after a BGP change), warning that an empty/small `accepted` table 3 minutes after a route-map change is ambiguous

Recommends recording the point-in-time snapshot timestamp and re-running the assessment ~15 minutes later after BGP route-view stabilization before treating all 340 prefixes as confirmed permanent gaps (while still flagging `empty_vifs` if it persists)

evals.prompt: On a Transit VIF attached via a DXGW to AWS Transit Gateway, we see exactly `200` `advertised` routes from AWS while 15 new spoke VPC CIDRs are missing on-premises; meanwhile, on another Private VIF, our datacenter team plans to advertise `140` on-premises IPv4 `/24` prefixes tomorrow without changing default VIF prefix settings. Explain what happens in both cases and how the two Direct Connect route quotas behave differently.
evals.expected_output: Activates dx-vif-resilience and contrasts: (1) `200` advertised prefixes (IPv4 + IPv6 combined) per DXGW↔TGW association on Transit VIFs—hitting 200 clips/omits additional prefixes (requiring prefix summarization or an AWS quota increase, vs 5,000 on Cloud WAN); (2) `100` accepted prefixes default per BGP session per address family on Private/Transit VIFs (self-service adjustable up to `1,000` via prefix controls / `UpdateVirtualInterfaceAttributes`)—exceeding 100 does NOT silently drop routes #101–140; instead it tears down the BGP session (`IDLE` / `DOWN`)!
expectations: Activates the dx-vif-resilience skill

Identifies the **`200` advertised prefix quota** (IPv4 + IPv6 combined per DXGW↔Transit Gateway association, compared to `5,000` on Cloud WAN), explaining why routes beyond 200 fail to advertise until summarized or increased

Identifies the **`100` accepted prefix default quota** per address family on Private/Transit VIFs (adjustable up to `1,000` via prefix controls) and warns that advertising 140 prefixes over the default 100 limit **drops the entire BGP session (`DOWN`/`IDLE`)** rather than silently truncating excess prefixes

evals.prompt: Across two redundant Private VIFs (`dxvif-01` and `dxvif-02`), both VIFs carry the exact same 45 prefixes, but `dxvif-01` tags them with BGP community `7224:7300` and AS-PATH `[65001]`, whereas `dxvif-02` tags them with `7224:7100` and AS-PATH `[65001, 65001, 65001]`. expectations: Activates the dx-vif-resilience skill

Classifies the 45 prefixes with `7224:7300` vs `7224:7100` local-preference communities and AS-PATH prepending as **`covered`** (deliberate active/passive traffic engineering, NOT a failover coverage gap)

Reports connection-derived checks (resiliency group and LAG membership) for the hosted cross-account VIFs as **`cannot verify (connection owned by another account)`** (`indeterminate`) rather than `'none'`, while noting VIF-level `awsLogicalDeviceId` and DX `location` checks remain valid

evals.prompt: In a Direct Connect audit of 3 VIFs: `dxvif-1` and `dxvif-2` belong to connections placed in the same Direct Connect Resiliency Group, but `DescribeConnections` shows `billingMode: FlatRateTier1` instead of `PortPairFlatRateTier1`, while `dxvif-3` (`available`, Transit VIF on `dxgw-999`) has no peer VIF on `dxgw-999`. evals.expected_output: Activates dx-vif-resilience and flags both structural findings: (1) declared-but-broken Resiliency Group pairing (`FlatRateTier*` inside a resiliency group instead of `PortPairFlatRateTier*` means speed/tier/device port-pair requirements are unmet so the connections are not actually paired by AWS), and (2) `no redundant peer detected for dxvif-3` (single point of failure with zero failover VIF).
expectations: Activates the dx-vif-resilience skill

Flags `FlatRateTier*` (instead of `PortPairFlatRateTier*`) inside a Direct Connect Resiliency Group as **declared-but-broken port pairing** (mismatched speed/tier/device preventing active AWS port-pair redundancy)
Flags lone `dxvif-3` explicitly as **`no redundant peer detected for dxvif-3`** (single-VIF SPOF)

evals.prompt: Check official AWS documentation to verify two AWS Direct Connect features outside route-symmetry checks: (1) what is the default AWS Direct Connect Bidirectional Forwarding Detection (BFD) liveness detection interval and multiplier (and is asynchronous BFD enabled automatically on AWS's side?), and (2) how does **AWS Direct Connect SiteLink** route traffic directly between two on-premises DX locations via a Direct Connect Gateway without hairpinning through an AWS Region VPC?
evals.expected_output: Activates dx-vif-resilience, queries awsknowledge / aws-mcp documentation tools for Direct Connect BFD and SiteLink, confirms AWS enables asynchronous BFD automatically on Direct Connect VIFs with a minimum AWS BFD interval of 300 ms and multiplier of 3 (~900 ms sub-second failure detection once enabled on the customer router), and explains enabling SiteLink (`enableSiteLink=true`) on Private/Transit VIFs attached to the same DXGW so on-premises offices exchange BGP routes directly across the global AWS backbone POP-to-POP.
expectations: Activates the dx-vif-resilience skill and queries connected AWS documentation MCP tools (awsknowledge or aws-mcp search_documentation / read_documentation) without running raw shell CLI commands

States AWS Direct Connect's BFD parameters accurately: asynchronous BFD is pre-enabled on the AWS side with a default/minimum `300 ms` interval and `3` liveness retries (~`900 ms` detection once configured on the on-prem router)

Explains AWS Direct Connect SiteLink: enabling `SiteLink` on Private or Transit VIFs attached to a shared Direct Connect Gateway routes office-to-office traffic shortest-path between DX POPs over the AWS backbone without traversing an AWS Region
